attribution.note: Marcus directly asserts that his earlier warnings are coming true.

semantics.note: The normalization preserves the retrospective assertion about the three named harms without adding a future prediction.

contract.note: The readings of web pollution, large-audience misinformation, and increased scam occurrence are ordinary and fair. Using 2025 reasonably anchors the ongoing conditions described in January 2026. Requiring AI involvement without sole causation fits the context.

evidence.note: Establishes earlier warnings about automated misinformation and web pollution, but neither their realization nor an earlier warning about increased cyberscams.
Documents low-quality, probably AI-generated content in a 2025 educational-video sample. Supports pollution in that setting; low prevalence and narrow coverage limit broader conclusions.
Documents large-scale dissemination of AI-enabled false narratives through March 2025. The cumulative figures include December 2024 and measure views rather than unique viewers or belief.

Vendor measurements show a declining identity-fraud rate since 2024 alongside changing techniques. This narrower population and metric do not establish or refute an increase in AI-enabled cyberscams overall.

Official 2025 figures establish AI-related complaints and increased total internet-crime complaints. The broader total and absence of a comparable earlier AI series prevent inferring increased AI-enabled scam occurrence.

reviews.rationale: The packet supports observed AI web pollution and large-audience misinformation. It does not establish a comparable increase in AI-enabled cyberscam occurrence or locate the earlier cyberscam warning. Narrow fraud-rate declines and limited slop prevalence do not contradict the overall assertion. The claim that all three warnings are coming true remains unsettled.
